hypothesis: An AI-specific operational resilience stack that combines meta-monitoring, calibrated early-warning thresholds, and codified AI-incident runbooks will (a) detect model degradation and collapse materially earlier and (b) reduce incident impact and resolution time versus a generic application monitoring setup, when evaluated on the same AI-dependent financial process under controlled failure scenarios.

baseline.description: Generic application monitoring for an AI-dependent financial process without AI-specific meta-monitoring or AI-incident runbooks.
characteristics: Standard infrastructure monitoring: CPU, memory, latency, error rates (e.g., HTTP 5xx), message queue lag.
Basic functional checks: service up/down, endpoint health checks returning HTTP 200.
No direct monitoring of model inputs, outputs, drift, uncertainty, or internal model signals.
No explicit AI early-warning indicators or tuned thresholds beyond generic service SLIs/SLOs.
Incident response follows generic IT incident process (e.g., severity levels, on-call engineer), with no AI-specific triage steps or decision criteria (e.g., when to roll back a model).
Logging is application-oriented (requests, responses, errors) without structured capture of AI-specific context (e.g., feature distributions, model version, decision rationale).
implementation_notes: Use a simple web service that wraps a pre-trained model (e.g., a binary classifier for credit approval) with REST API.
Attach standard monitoring (Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, or equivalent) to capture uptime, latency, and error counts only.
Configure a single generic alert: e.g., 'alert if 5xx_error_rate_5m > 2% of requests for 10 minutes'.
Use a minimal runbook: 'If alert fires, investigate logs, restart service, escalate to on-call data scientist if needed' with no AI-specific steps.

treatment.description: Enhanced AI-aware operational resilience setup that adds model-level meta-monitoring, AI-specific early warning indicators, and a structured AI-incident runbook on top of the same baseline infrastructure.
components: AI Early Warning Metrics (Section 9.2):
- Input data monitoring: population drift (e.g., PSI or JS divergence) versus recent baseline; missing/invalid feature rate.
- Output monitoring: approval/rejection rate distribution, score distribution drift, calibration shifts.
- Outcome proxy monitoring: short-term realized default/charge-off proxies using lagged labels in synthetic workloads.
Model Meta-Monitoring (Section 9.3):
- Prediction uncertainty monitoring (e.g., predicted probability near 0.5 band, entropy-based score).
- Stability monitoring across models: divergence between champion and shadow model outputs on a sampled subset.
- Internal consistency checks: monotonicity checks on selected features, simple rule-based backstops.
Alerting and Thresholds (Sections 9.2, 9.3):
- Multi-tier thresholds (info, warning, critical) defined on AI-specific metrics, e.g.:
* PSI(input_feature_x) > 0.2 for 30 minutes => warning; > 0.3 => critical.
* Drop in approval rate > 30% relative to 7-day rolling average => critical.
* Champion-shadow disagreement rate > 20% for 15 minutes => warning.
- Alert aggregation rules to avoid alert storms and prioritize business-critical indicators.
AI Incident Runbook (Section 9.4):
- Triage steps: identify whether issue is infra, data pipeline, or model-behavior driven using defined diagnostic queries.
- Decision tree for containment: when to throttle traffic, revert to previous model, switch to fallback rule-based logic, or invoke manual review mode.
- Pre-defined communication templates for operations, risk management, and compliance teams.
Business Continuity Modes (Section 9.5):
- Configurable fallback strategies:
* Fallback to last-known-good model version.
* Fallback to conservative rule-based decisioning.
* Fallback to manual review for a capped volume of high-value transactions.
Integration with Incident Management (Sections 9.6, 9.7):
- Auto-tagging of incidents as 'AI-model' vs 'infra' in an incident tracker (e.g., Jira, ServiceNow-like stub).
- Automatic attachment of model monitoring snapshots and key metrics to incident records.
Readiness Testing Harness (Section 9.8):
- Scripts to inject controlled failures (data drift, label shift, model parameter corruption) and to replay historical-like stress scenarios.
- Logging of detection time, triggered alerts, actions taken (simulated), and time to recovery.
implementation_notes: Reuse the same service and model as the baseline; instrument additional AI metrics in a sidecar collector process.
Implement early-warning calculations (PSI, approval-rate deltas, disagreement rates) in a streaming or micro-batch fashion (e.g., every 1–5 minutes).
Define alerting rules in the same monitoring stack as baseline (e.g., Prometheus alertmanager rules, or a Python-based rules engine).
Formalize the AI incident runbook as structured YAML/JSON plus markdown, and reference it in code for automated actions (e.g., simulated switch to fallback).

workloads.name: WL1_normal_operations
workloads.description: Simulated normal operations for an AI-based credit approval model under stable conditions.
steps: Generate or load a synthetic but realistic tabular dataset representing credit applications with features such as income, utilization, age, delinquency indicators.
Train a baseline binary classifier (e.g., gradient boosting or logistic regression) to produce approval probabilities; fix its weights before experiments.
Deploy the model as an inference service accessible via a simple API or batch function.
Stream requests at a steady rate (e.g., 20–100 requests per second) for a sustained period (e.g., 60 minutes).
Ensure data distribution matches the model's training distribution, with stable approval and default rates.
Record all monitoring metrics under both baseline and treatment setups; no induced faults.
Use WL1 primarily for calibration of thresholds and as a control to measure false positive alert rates.
workloads.purpose: Validate that the enhanced AI monitoring does not generate excessive false positives under normal, stable conditions and that incident runbooks are not inadvertently triggered.

workloads.name: WL2_gradual_data_drift
workloads.description: Gradual but material drift in input features and target distribution for an AI credit model over multiple hours, mimicking a slow macroeconomic regime change.
steps: Start with WL1-like traffic for an initial warm-up period (e.g., 20 minutes).
Over the next 60–120 minutes, slowly alter key input feature distributions, e.g.:
- Increase average utilization and debt-to-income ratio.
- Change the geographic or segment mix of applications.
- Introduce gradual changes in correlation between features.

Simultaneously, alter labels (for lagged outcome simulation) to reflect a worsening credit environment (higher default rates), with labels becoming observable after a defined lag (e.g., 15 minutes in simulated time).
Keep infrastructure health stable (no added latency, no 5xx errors) so failures appear only at the model/decision layer.
Run baseline and treatment configurations separately but with identical random seeds and drift schedule.
Log when each configuration first exhibits materially degraded performance (e.g., captured via a hidden 'oracle' metric like true AUC on the drifting distribution), and when/if alerts fire.
For the treatment, simulate runbook execution choices when critical thresholds are breached (e.g., switching to a more conservative model).
workloads.purpose: Test whether AI-specific early-warning metrics detect degradation significantly earlier than generic infra metrics, and whether codified runbooks enable faster and more consistent containment actions.

workloads.name: WL3_abrupt_model_corruption
workloads.description: Sudden, catastrophic degradation of the model due to configuration error or corrupted weights, with infrastructure otherwise healthy.
steps: Run WL1 for an initial period (e.g., 10–15 minutes) to establish baseline behavior.
At a specific time T0, introduce a model-level fault such as:
- Swapping the model with a poorly trained or random-weight model.
- Shuffling model coefficients.
- Applying an incorrect pre-processing pipeline (e.g., permuting key features).
Keep API latency and uptime within normal limits to avoid obvious infra alarms.
Continue sending traffic at the same rate for at least 30–45 minutes after T0.
Compute an 'oracle' quality metric (e.g., AUC or error rate) offline using true labels to quantify underlying severity.

For baseline and treatment, measure time from T0 to first fired alert; in treatment, track which AI-specific metrics triggered alerts (e.g., approval rate collapse, extreme score distributions, champion-shadow disagreement).
For treatment, simulate application of the runbook: e.g., immediate rollback to previous model version or switch to manual review for high-risk segments.

Capture the volume and value of misclassified decisions between T0 and containment in both conditions (e.g., funds misallocated, approvals wrongly given/denied) using synthetic financial impact rules.
workloads.purpose: Evaluate the speed and quality of detection and response to abrupt model failures, where generic infra metrics provide little signal but AI-aware meta-monitoring should be highly sensitive.

workloads.name: WL4_upstream_data_vendor_failure
workloads.description: Degradation and partial corruption of upstream data from an external vendor (e.g., bureau data), leading to flawed model inputs even though the model and hosting infra remain technically sound.
steps: Simulate normal traffic for an initial period with all features correctly populated, including a 'vendor_feature_block'.
At time T1, inject issues specifically in vendor-related fields:
- Spike in missing values (e.g., 50–90% becoming null).
- Static or frozen values (no variability over time).
- Abnormal categorical codes not seen in training.
Ensure generic infra metrics remain normal (no HTTP errors or abnormal latencies).
Allow the system to continue processing for 45–60 minutes under corrupted input conditions.
Under the treatment system, configure input quality metrics and vendor-specific data quality checks (e.g., vendor_feature_missing_rate, vendor_feature_entropy).
Run the scenario under baseline and treatment with identical seeds and failure injections.

Log detection times, alert context (which metrics fired), and simulated response actions (e.g., switching to backup vendor data, invoking manual review, or applying conservative overrides where vendor data is missing).
workloads.purpose: Test whether AI-specific input quality and external dependency monitoring allow faster detection and more targeted response to third-party data failures compared to generic monitoring.

execution_controls: Run baseline and treatment experiments on the same hardware and software stack, differing only in monitoring/alerting and incident automation components.
Use fixed random seeds for data generation, label assignment, and failure injection to ensure identical workloads across baseline and treatment.
Ensure consistent model training (same hyperparameters and pre-processing) prior to divergence at runtime.
Disable any self-healing cloud features that would mask failures (e.g., automatic restarts based solely on infra metrics) or apply them identically in both baseline and treatment.
Ensure that no human-in-the-loop manual interventions are made during runtime unless explicitly scripted and simulated as part of the AI runbook in the treatment condition.
Keep logging verbosity and retention the same for baseline and treatment to avoid bias in subsequent analysis.
measurement_controls: Synchronize clocks and timestamps across monitoring systems to allow precise calculation of detection and containment intervals.
Log all alerts with a standardized schema including metric name, threshold, severity, timestamp, and associated workload identifier.
Record ground-truth 'oracle' model performance metrics (e.g., AUC, error rate) and synthetic financial impact metrics using the same evaluation pipeline for baseline and treatment.
Record which fallback or continuity actions were triggered (real or simulated) with timestamps to reconstruct the full incident timeline.
Use blinded analysis scripts that compute metrics based on logs without knowing whether they originated from baseline or treatment runs until after metrics are calculated.

metrics.name: time_to_detection
metrics.definition: Elapsed wall-clock time between the known failure injection timestamp (T0/T1) and the first alert that correctly signals AI-related degradation (model or input-level) for a given incident scenario.

metrics.name: time_to_containment_decision
metrics.definition: Elapsed time between failure injection and the point at which a containment action decision is logged (e.g., simulated rollback, switch to fallback, or traffic throttling) according to the runbook.

metrics.name: time_to_stable_recovery
metrics.definition: Elapsed time between failure injection and restoration of metrics to within a defined band of pre-incident baselines (e.g., approval rates, error rates, drift measures), sustained for a minimum stabilization window (e.g., 15 minutes).

metrics.name: false_positive_alert_rate
metrics.definition: Number of AI-related alerts triggered during WL1_normal_operations per hour that are not associated with any injected failure conditions.

metrics.name: missed_detection_rate
metrics.definition: Fraction of failure injections where no AI-related alert fires within a maximum acceptable detection window (e.g., 30 minutes for gradual drift, 5 minutes for abrupt corruption).

metrics.name: cumulative_misclassified_decisions
metrics.definition: Number of decisions (e.g., loan approvals/denials) that differ from those of a 'gold standard' reference model or policy between failure injection and containment, indicating the volume of impacted decisions.

metrics.name: estimated_incident_financial_impact
metrics.definition: Aggregate estimated financial loss (e.g., expected credit loss from mispriced approvals, opportunity cost of overly conservative denials) computed using synthetic but consistent loss rules across conditions.

metrics.name: operator_runbook_adherence
metrics.definition: Proportion of prescribed runbook steps that are followed in correct order and within target time bounds during incident simulations, based on logs or scenario scripts; for baseline, this may be near-zero where runbooks are generic or absent.

metrics.name: alert_precision
metrics.definition: Among all AI-related alerts fired across workloads, the fraction that correspond to times with actual, injected failures or objectively confirmed AI degradations (defined by 'oracle' metrics crossing severity thresholds).

metrics.name: alert_lead_time_vs_oracle
metrics.definition: Difference between the time when an 'oracle' quality metric crosses a severe degradation threshold and the time when the first AI alert fires (negative values indicate earlier alerts than oracle crossing).

success_criteria: For gradual drift (WL2), median time_to_detection under the treatment configuration is at least 50% lower than under the baseline configuration, with no more than a 2x increase in false_positive_alert_rate during WL1_normal_operations.

For abrupt model corruption (WL3), 95th percentile time_to_detection under treatment is less than or equal to 120 seconds, while baseline either fails to detect within 10 minutes (missed_detection) or detects significantly later.

For upstream data vendor failure (WL4), treatment demonstrates a missed_detection_rate at least 50% lower than baseline and a statistically significant reduction in estimated_incident_financial_impact (e.g., p < 0.05 under a suitable non-parametric test using repeated runs).
Across WL2–WL4, treatment achieves a cumulative_misclassified_decisions that is at least 30% lower than baseline for the same workloads and injected failures.

Under WL1_normal_operations, alert_precision under treatment is at least 0.8 and false_positive_alert_rate remains below a pre-defined operational tolerance (e.g., <= 2 AI-specific alerts per 8-hour equivalent).
Operator_runbook_adherence in treatment scenario drills exceeds 0.9, demonstrating that the structured AI incident runbooks are actionable and consistently followed within the simulation framework.

failure_modes.name: overly_sensitive_thresholds
failure_modes.description: Early-warning thresholds set too tightly generate frequent alerts during WL1_normal_operations, leading to high false_positive_alert_rate and undermining practical usability.
mitigations: Use WL1 and early WL2 phases to empirically calibrate thresholds to target alert_precision >= 0.8.
Apply hysteresis and rolling windows to smooth metrics and avoid reacting to transient noise.
Conduct sensitivity analysis by sweeping threshold parameters and re-running WL1 to find balanced settings.

failure_modes.name: silent_failure_in_monitoring_pipeline
failure_modes.description: Monitoring or metric computation fails (e.g., sidecar crash, feature logging error), resulting in missing or stale indicators and giving a false sense of security.
mitigations: Implement health checks and heartbeat metrics for the monitoring components themselves (meta-monitoring).
Alert on absence of expected monitoring data streams (e.g., no metric updates for > N minutes).
Log monitoring pipeline errors separately and include them in experiment evaluation to detect bias.

failure_modes.name: confounding_infra_issues
failure_modes.description: Unintended infrastructure issues (e.g., network latency spikes) occur during AI failure injections, causing baseline monitoring to detect incidents based on infra symptoms and obscuring AI detection performance differences.
mitigations: Isolate the experimental environment with stable, controlled resources.
Monitor and log infra metrics explicitly and tag runs where infra anomalies exceed predefined thresholds; exclude or separately analyze these runs.
Optionally replay workloads purely as offline logs through monitoring logic to decouple infra behavior from AI behavior.

failure_modes.name: label_leakage_in_oracle_metrics
failure_modes.description: Oracle metrics or synthetic financial impact calculations inadvertently use future information or leak labels in a way that would not be available in real time, invalidating lead-time comparisons.
mitigations: Strictly enforce label lags in oracle metric computation to mirror realistic feedback delays.
Separate online monitoring metrics (which must not see future labels) from offline evaluation metrics in the codebase.
Review metric computation pipelines for potential leakage during code review and unit testing.

failure_modes.name: unrealistic_synthetic_data_or_scenarios
failure_modes.description: Synthetic workloads and failure injections do not resemble realistic financial services patterns, limiting external validity of conclusions.
mitigations: Base data generation parameters on published benchmarks, anonymized institution-level aggregates, or domain SME input.
Vary multiple scenario parameters (drift magnitude, vendor outage duration, traffic levels) and report sensitivity of results.
Document scenario assumptions clearly to aid interpretation and adaptation to real-world environments.

failure_modes.name: runbook_complexity_and_non-use
failure_modes.description: The AI incident runbooks become too complex to be followed even in simulation, leading to low operator_runbook_adherence despite technical monitoring improvements.
mitigations: Keep runbooks compact and decision-tree based, with a limited number of branches for common incident types.
Dry-run runbooks with technical teams and simplify steps that are frequently skipped or misunderstood.
Log not only which steps are executed but also decision justifications to inform iterative refinement.

hardware: Commodity server or cloud instance with at least 4 CPU cores, 16 GB RAM, and 50 GB of available storage for logs and data.
Optional GPU is not required; models can be small tabular classifiers.
software_stack: Data/ML libraries: pandas, numpy, scikit-learn (or similar), scipy.
Monitoring and metrics stack: Prometheus + Alertmanager (or an equivalent metrics store and alerting engine), or a Python-native monitoring library with time-series persistence.
Logging: structured logging via Python logging or similar, with JSON output.
Containerization (optional but recommended): Docker to package model service, monitoring sidecar, and workload generator.
Orchestration (optional): docker-compose or Kubernetes for orchestrating baseline vs treatment deployments.
Version control: git, with repository structure aligned to https://github.com/bookauthority/boardroom-blind-spots.
Configuration management: YAML/JSON-based configuration files to define thresholds, alert rules, and runbook mappings.
data: Synthetic tabular dataset representing credit applications, generated via provided scripts or loaded from an open dataset compatible with financial-like modeling (e.g., credit-scoring-style data, appropriately anonymized).
Definition of synthetic label generation rules and financial impact mapping (e.g., expected loss models) that are consistent across baseline and treatment.
Configuration files for each workload scenario detailing drift schedules, failure injection times, and vendor data failure patterns.
security_and_compliance: Use only synthetic or fully anonymized data with no personal identifiable information.
Run experiments in a non-production environment isolated from live customer systems.
Review and align the experimental setup with internal model risk and operational resilience policies before using institution-specific data.

run_instructions: 1. Clone Repository and Set Up Environment:
- Clone the repository: git clone https://github.com/bookauthority/boardroom-blind-spots.git
- Navigate to the chapter 9 experiment directory (e.g., experiments/ch09_operational_resilience/).
- Create and activate a Python virtual environment.
- Install dependencies: pip install -r requirements.txt
2. Generate or Load Synthetic Data:
- Run the data generation script (e.g., python scripts/generate_synthetic_credit_data.py) to create a base training and evaluation dataset.
- Optionally adjust configuration (configs/data_generation.yaml) to change portfolio size, feature distributions, and base default rates.
3. Train and Freeze the Baseline Model:
- Execute the training script (e.g., python scripts/train_baseline_model.py --config configs/model/baseline.yaml).
- Confirm that the trained model artifact is saved to the designated models/ directory with a version identifier.
4. Deploy Baseline Service and Monitoring:
- Start the model inference service in baseline mode (e.g., docker-compose -f docker-compose-baseline.yaml up or python services/model_service.py --mode baseline).
- Start the baseline monitoring stack (e.g., Prometheus, Alertmanager, and any exporters defined in monitoring/baseline/).
- Verify that health endpoints and baseline metrics (latency, error rate) are being scraped and stored.
5. Configure and Run Workloads Under Baseline Setup:
- For each workload (WL1–WL4), review and, if needed, edit scenario configuration files under configs/workloads/ (e.g., wl1_normal.yaml, wl2_drift.yaml).
- Run the workload generator for WL1 (e.g., python workloads/run_workload.py --config configs/workloads/wl1_normal.yaml --mode baseline).
- Repeat for WL2, WL3, and WL4, ensuring that each run produces logs and metrics tagged with workload_id and mode=baseline.
6. Deploy Treatment Service with AI Meta-Monitoring:
- Start the enhanced model inference service with monitoring sidecar (e.g., docker-compose -f docker-compose-treatment.yaml up or python services/model_service.py --mode treatment).
- Start the AI-specific metrics collector (e.g., python monitoring/ai_metrics_collector.py --config configs/monitoring/ai_metrics.yaml).
- Start the alerting/rules engine with treatment-specific rules (e.g., Prometheus Alertmanager using rules in monitoring/treatment/rules.yml or a Python rules engine script).
7. Configure AI-Specific Thresholds and Runbooks:
- Edit configs/monitoring/thresholds.yaml to set PSI, approval-rate, disagreement-rate, and other thresholds, using WL1 calibration results if available.
- Define AI incident runbooks in configs/runbooks/ (e.g., standardized YAML with steps and triggers).
8. Run Workloads Under Treatment Setup:
- Repeat Step 5 for WL1–WL4, but run the workload generator with --mode treatment and ensure identical random seeds and scenario config apart from mode.
- Confirm that AI-specific metrics are logged and that alerts are being generated according to the configured rules.
- For WL2–WL4, ensure that simulated runbook actions (e.g., switch_to_fallback) are logged with timestamps when triggered by alerts.
9. Collect and Consolidate Evidence:
- Use provided scripts (e.g., python analysis/aggregate_logs.py) to merge logs from baseline and treatment runs into standardized evidence JSON/CSV files adhering to the evidence_schema.
- Ensure each record includes experiment_id, workload_id, mode (baseline/treatment), timestamps, alert details, and oracle metrics.
10. Analyze Metrics and Compare Baseline vs Treatment:

- Run analysis scripts (e.g., python analysis/compute_metrics.py --config configs/analysis/metrics.yaml) to compute time_to_detection, cumulative_misclassified_decisions, estimated_incident_financial_impact, and other defined metrics for each run.
- Use statistical comparison scripts (e.g., python analysis/compare_conditions.py) to summarize differences between baseline and treatment across repeated runs.
11. Document Findings and Map to Book Content:
- Export summary tables and plots to reports/ (e.g., detection_time_comparison.png, financial_impact_boxplots.png).
- Link specific findings back to Chapter 9 sections (e.g., how early-warning metrics in 9.2 reduced time_to_detection in WL2) for inclusion in board-level materials.
12. Optional: Extend Scenarios for Institution-Specific Context:
- Adapt workload configurations and loss models to reflect institution-specific AI use cases (e.g., fraud detection, trading signals) while maintaining the same experimental structure.
- Re-run experiments and analyses to calibrate AI operational resilience controls to the institution's own environment.

evidence_schema.description: Standardized schema for logging and analyzing experiment runs, alerts, and outcomes for both baseline and treatment configurations.

top_level_fields.name: experiment_id
top_level_fields.description: Identifier of the experiment specification associated with this evidence record.

top_level_fields.name: run_id
top_level_fields.description: Unique identifier for a single execution of a workload under a given mode.

top_level_fields.name: mode
top_level_fields.description: Indicates whether the run used the generic monitoring baseline or AI-enhanced treatment setup.

top_level_fields.name: config_version
top_level_fields.description: Version identifier of the configuration bundle (monitoring thresholds, runbooks, workload parameters) used for this run.

top_level_fields.name: failure_injections

fields.name: injection_id
fields.description: Identifier for the injected failure.

fields.name: failure_type
fields.description: Categorical description of failure (e.g., data_drift, model_corruption, vendor_data_failure).

fields.name: injection_time
fields.description: Timestamp when the failure was first applied.

fields.name: parameters
fields.description: Key-value map of parameters controlling the failure (e.g., drift_magnitude, missing_rate).

top_level_fields.description: List of induced failures and their properties for this run.

top_level_fields.name: alerts

fields.name: alert_id
fields.description: Unique identifier of the alert event.

fields.name: timestamp
fields.description: Time at which the alert was generated.

fields.name: metric_name
fields.description: Name of the metric that triggered the alert.

fields.name: metric_value
fields.description: Value of the metric at alert triggering time.

fields.name: threshold
fields.description: Configured threshold associated with the alert.

fields.name: severity
fields.description: Severity level of the alert.

fields.name: category
fields.description: High-level categorization of the alert.

fields.name: related_injection_id
fields.description: If applicable, the injection_id this alert is associated with, for labeling true/false positives.

top_level_fields.description: All alerts raised during the run, including those not tied to injected failures.

top_level_fields.name: runbook_actions

fields.name: action_id
fields.description: Unique identifier for the logged runbook action.

fields.name: timestamp
fields.description: Time at which the action was taken (or simulated).

fields.name: action_type
fields.description: Categorical type of action (e.g., notify_risk_team, rollback_model, enable_manual_review).

fields.name: triggering_alert_id
fields.description: ID of the alert that directly triggered this action, if any.

fields.name: runbook_step_id
fields.description: Identifier referring to the prescribed runbook step executed.

fields.name: metadata
fields.description: Additional structured details (e.g., parameters of fallback, fraction of traffic rerouted).

top_level_fields.description: Sequence of actions taken under the AI incident runbooks during the run.

top_level_fields.name: oracle_metrics_time_series

fields.name: timestamp
fields.description: Time at which the oracle metrics were computed (may be lagged).

fields.name: auc
fields.description: Computed AUC of the model at this time window, using realized labels.

fields.name: error_rate
fields.description: Misclassification rate over the recent time window.

fields.name: financial_impact_rate
fields.description: Estimated financial impact per unit time (e.g., per minute) based on synthetic loss rules.

top_level_fields.description: Time series of oracle performance and impact metrics for post-hoc analysis and ground truth comparison.

top_level_fields.name: aggregated_outcomes

fields.name: time_to_detection
fields.description: Computed for each injected failure as earliest relevant alert time minus injection time; null if missed.

fields.name: time_to_containment_decision
fields.description: Time from injection to first containment-related runbook action; null if none.

fields.name: time_to_stable_recovery
fields.description: Time from injection to stable metric recovery; null if stability criterion not achieved in run.

fields.name: false_positive_alert_count
fields.description: Number of alerts not associated with any injected failure or oracle-defined degradation crossing thresholds.

fields.name: cumulative_misclassified_decisions
fields.description: Total number of misclassified decisions during the run relative to a gold-standard model/policy.

fields.name: estimated_incident_financial_impact
fields.description: Total estimated financial impact across the run, aggregated from oracle_metrics_time_series and decision logs.

fields.name: operator_runbook_adherence
fields.description: Fraction of prescribed runbook steps correctly executed; null if no runbook defined (e.g., baseline).

fields.name: alert_precision
fields.description: Fraction of alerts that correspond to actual injected failures or oracle-defined degradations.

top_level_fields.description: Derived summary metrics for each run, used to evaluate success criteria.
